documents/pages/physical-education.pdf.text: October 2020 SIXTH FORM: Physical Education PE A Level Course Overview Students will undertake a broad programme of study that develops their understanding of the factors that influence sporting performance. Year 12 begins with an exploration of Exercise Physiology, Skill Acquisition, Sport Psychology and Sport & Society, providing the foundations for success throughout the course. Through theoretical and practical learning experiences, students will develop their knowledge of the human body, the learning and performance of skills, and the social and psychological influences on participation and achievement in sport. Students will build their analytical, evaluative and extended-writing skills through the application of theory to real sporting situations and performance examples. As the course progresses, students will refine their practical performance and begin developing the skills required for their Non-Examined Assessment, applying theoretical concepts to analyse and improve performance. This prepares students for the demands of A Level study and progression into higher education, coaching, teaching, sports science and a range of related careers. What’s great about Art at Tenison’s Sixth Form? Students thrive in the PE department through a balance of engaging practical experiences and challenging academic study. Our classes are smaller than those at GCSE, allowing students to benefit from personalised support, expert guidance and regular feedback from experienced teachers. The department consistently performs above the national average, reflecting the high levels of achievement and support on offer. The department provides a unique opportunity to apply theoretical knowledge in practical settings, helping students develop as performers, coaches and analysts. Lessons are welcoming, supportive and collaborative, creating an environment where students feel confident to succeed, enjoy their learning and reach their full potential. Opportunities and Successes • A wide range of opportunities to develop leadership skills through coaching, officiating and supporting sporting events across the school community. • Fostering a lifelong passion for sport, physical activity and wellbeing that extends far beyond Sixth Form. • Previous students have progressed onto a variety of sport-related university courses and careers, with many returning to share their experiences and inspire the next generation of students.

documents/pages/prospectus.pdf.text: Archbishop Tenison’s Founded by Thomas Tenison, Archbishop of Canterbury, in 1714, the school was designed to give “ten poor boys and ten poor girls” a good basic education to help them earn an honest living and grow in the Christian faith. Today it is an 11-18 voluntary aided, mixed, Anglican comprehensive school within the Diocese of Southwark and the Borough of Croydon, with Foundation Governors appointed by the Church of England. Archbishop Tenison’s offers an academic Sixth Form Curriculum with a wide range of A-Levels and extra-curricular activities. The Sixth Form is a small community with around 100 students. Students are known individually and enabled to flourish with the support and guidance needed over their two years of study. We have students from many different schools and welcome applicants from all backgrounds. Archbishop Tenison’s is an Anglican foundation, so students are expected to be sympathetic to the ideals which underlie our Christian ethos. “Our sixth form is a place that encourages both academic and personal growth. It offers a wide range of opportunities, but what truly makes it exceptional is the supportive community and inspiring environment. Here, students are challenged, guided, and motivated to reach their potential, leaving well prepared for the next stage of their journey.” Zain, Year 13 The Sixth Form The Sixth Form years are a unique opportunity to learn academically, develop personally and socially, and discuss your calling and way ahead for your future. We are rightly proud of the great contribution our Sixth Formers make to the whole community. We recognise that every Sixth Form student has to work hard, rise to considerable challenges in their studies and make the most of many extra-curricular opportunities too. We also hope that by pursuing your post-16 studies at this school, you will develop not just into a person of great character but one who can make a difference to the wider world in which we live. “Archbishop Tenison’s Sixth Form is a caring atmosphere full of friendly people, with a strong community feel. The staff are kind and never hesitate to help wherever they can. All subjects are taught with enthusiasm and passion. The Sixth Form offers not just a wide range of subjects but also many extra-curricular activities which are always enjoyable and rewarding.” Daniel, Year 12 Why Study at Tenison’s Archbishop Tenison’s has a strong academic tradition, with a history of producing good results, and many of our students progress to the top universities. We offer a wide range of A-level subjects, full details of which can be found in the Course Guide. Students follow a two-year course, usually beginning with three subjects plus the Extended Project Qualification (EPQ), which is equivalent to AS-Level UCAS points. One of the hallmarks of our school is the way in which students work together. There is a strong sense of community within our Sixth Form and students are encouraged to participate in a range of activities beyond the formal curriculum, including music, drama, sport, business related workshops and public speaking. There are plenty of opportunities to develop leadership qualities through our mentoring programme and Sixth Form Council, as Student Leaders or as representatives on committees in school or the wider Croydon community. Life in the Sixth Form From the time of making your subject choices and attending interview through the induction programme and enrolment process, to progressing from being a pupil to a student, the school provides strong support for you through the challenges of these two formative years. We have a pastoral team of dedicated tutors who take an interest in the development of each individual. Learning to work together with others is an important aspect of our Sixth Form and students work together to prepare themselves for the challenges of life beyond the Sixth Form. “Archbishop Tenison’s is where futures begin to take shape. A wide range of subjects are available to all, and the school is more than just a learning environment - it is a community of unique, driven and immensely supportive people. Sixth Form Students cannot help but feel welcome as well as confident about taking the next steps towards their futures.” Aaliyah, Year 12 The sixth-form centre provides the perfect environment where students can socialise with their peers. We support students’ health and social needs through our tutorial programme. Students with a disability or Special Educational Need are well supported and successfully encouraged to fulfil their potential. Sixth Formers have their own assemblies and services and take part in formal occasions such as Founder’s Day. “Throughout my time at Tenison’s, the school has given me tailored support in all my subjects. They have allowed me to attend online classes when I have not been able to get into school due to mobility ailments. The school has been supportive throughout and continuously provided the help that I need. They have been very gracious to the fact that I may, at times, not be able to make it into school.” Izzy, Year 13 Expectations and Responsibilities We seek to instil our students with a sense of honesty and integrity which involves individuals taking responsibility for their own personal development and progression. Students will be offered the opportunity to widen their experiences of leading and influencing others. Underlying and supporting this aim is a positive Christian purpose that provides both direction and commitment for the school. Dress code involves wearing professional style clothing reflecting the position of the students in the school as its senior members. Teaching and Independent Learning Both depth and breadth of study are important in the Sixth Form. Our traditional, academic curriculum prepares students for popular courses in the best universities; our new courses prepare students for the wider range of degrees and employment. Inspirational teaching encourages students to engage in their subjects and provides the encouragement and environment for independent learning. Independent learning is the key to success at A-Level. A structured start helps students develop academic confidence, motivation and self-discipline. Individual advice, too, often makes the difference in the transition from GCSE to AS-Level. Our priority is to give students the tools of research, planning and evaluation which they need to organise their own learning. “The Sixth Form is good. Students are positive about the high-quality teaching they receive”. Ofsted Extra Curricular Activities Our Sixth Form students participate in a wide range of activities and enrichment courses designed for personal development. Paired Reading and Mentoring of Lower School pupils increases confidence and inter-personal skills. Debating and other competitions challenge students to perform at the highest level whilst Enrichment Days and Religious Studies Away Days will broaden an individual’s horizons. The opportunity to follow intensive Chartered Management Institute courses allow students to work together with leading business professionals. Working towards the Duke of Edinburgh Awards builds up skills, resilience and confidence. Stunning concerts involve the orchestra, wind band, choir and gospel, chamber and Sixth Form Singers. Drama and school productions help students to discover hidden talents. The Sixth Form Council runs a whole variety of events including the Annual Charity Appeal, the Revue (Soirée) and a variety of Sixth Form social events. The Christian character is a core part of life at Tenison’s. We have a welcoming atmosphere where young people come together to express and live out their faith. It is also a space where questions are asked about God to deepen personal understanding of Christianity. Joining will ensure those of the Christian faith can worship the Lord in spirit and in truth.” Sarina, Year 13 Communication Regular monitoring, evaluation and progress checks are carried out throughout the year. Parents/carers are invited to attend a Parents’ Consultation Evening and Higher Education Evening. Mutual communication is encouraged between home and school to support students’ learning and development. Making an Application This is an ‘Open Sixth Form’ and details on how to make an application are on our website. All students who accept our conditional offers are invited to an Insight Programme where they have the opportunity to experience teaching in the subjects that they have initially chosen and meet the current Sixth Form students. This programme takes place in early July for one week. After the GCSE results are published, students attend for enrolment where they finalise their choice of subjects. Further Information about the school, the admission criteria and application forms are available on the school website at: www.archten.croydon.sch.uk Archbishop Tenison’s CE High School Selborne Road, Croydon, CR0 5JQ Tel: 020 8688 4014 Email: sixthformadmissions@archten.croydon.sch.uk @archten archbishoptenisons /archtencroydon

documents/pages/pupil-premium-link-to-ou.text: Archbishop Tenison’s C of E High School Pupil premium strategy statement This statement details our school’s use of pupil premium funding to help improve the attainment of our disadvantaged pupils. It outlines our pupil premium strategy, how we intend to spend the funding in this academic year and the effect that last year’s spending of pupil premium had within our school. School overview Detail School name Number of pupils in school Proportion (%) of pupil premium eligible pupils Academic year/years that our current pupil premium strategy plan covers Date this statement was published Date on which it will be reviewed Statement authorised by Pupil premium lead Governor / Trustee lead Data Archbishop Tenison’s School 750 36% 2023/24-2025/26 February 2026 December 2026 Richard Parrish, Headteacher Lucie Philips Karen Bryson Funding overview Detail Pupil premium funding allocation this academic year Pupil premium funding carried forward from previous years (enter £0 if not applicable) Total budget for this academic year If your school is an academy in a trust that pools this funding, state the amount available to your school this academic year Amount £275,200 £0 £275,200 1 Part A: Pupil premium strategy plan Statement of intent Archbishop Tenison’s is committed to educating all pupils to the highest possible standard, irrespective of their academic or social background. As a church school, it is an integral part of our Christian vision to offer our disadvantaged pupils the same life chances as their peers. We endeavour to devote appropriate strategies, support and intervention to enable disadvantaged students to fulfil their academic and emotional potential during their time at the school. The primary focus of our strategy is ensuring high quality teaching, which is for the benefit all pupils, but is proven by evidence to have a disproportionately high impact on the progress of disadvantaged pupils. Our intention is to narrow the gap between the progress made by disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged pupils at the school, using Progress 8 scores at GCSE as the most appropriate measure of this aim. We are employing a range of strategies to make sure that our disadvantaged students can thrive within the classroom. We are using Pupil Premium funding to facilitate smaller classes in core subjects at Key Stage 3 and Key Stage 4, so that students can benefit from an improved teacher to student ratio. We have a dedicated pupil support room, with academic interventions starting from Year 7 students who we have identified as being at risk of not making the expected progress. As a small school, we are particularly well placed to offer individual, bespoke assistance to our disadvantaged pupils according to their needs. We have witnessed an increase in students with behavioural, social, emotional and mental health needs since the Covid pandemic. Our Pupil Support room and Welfare Hub provide vital assistance and interventions for students to improve their wellbeing and ensure that they are able to achieve well in school. We are also investing in mentoring and counselling from external organisations for our students with a high level of need. We are committed to offering all pupils a well-rounded and broad education, including a range of enrichment activities. It is our strong belief that all pupils should have access to learning opportunities beyond the classroom and that these activities are valuable in increasing pupils’ cultural capital. Our approach therefore also includes support to help students access extra curricular activities such as music lessons, trips, sports clubs and the Duke of Edinburgh scheme, allowing our disadvantaged students are able to take part fully in the wider life of the school. 2 Challenges This details the key challenges to achievement that we have identified among our disadvantaged pupils. Challenge number 1 2 3 4 5 Detail of challenge The 2025 GCSE results showed a gap in progress between non-PPG pupils and PPG pupils of -0.59. In English, the progress of PPG pupils was -0.49 compared with +0.03 of non-PPG pupils. In Maths the progress of PPG pupils was -0.72 compared with -0.09 for non-PPG pupils. The Progress 8 score of our disadvantaged pupils with low prior attainment at GCSE in 2025 was below that of their peers. Our internal testing has identified a gap in Maths and English attainment between disadvantaged pupils and the rest of the cohort in Year 7. There was a gap of 5% between the attendance of our disadvantaged pupils compared to their peers in the academic year 2023/2024. There has been an increase in the number of PPG students with SEMH needs, impacting students’ wellbeing and attendance. Intended outcomes This explains the outcomes we are aiming for by the end of our current strategy plan, and how we will measure whether they have been achieved. Intended outcome Improved attainment among disadvantaged pupils at KS4, particularly in English and Maths. Improved attainment for disadvantaged pupils with lower and low-mid prior attainment across the curriculum at GCSE. Disadvantaged pupils in Year 7 and 8 make good progress in English and Maths. Improved attendance of disadvantaged pupils across KS3 and 4. Excellent pastoral support for disadvantaged pupils. Disadvantaged pupils engaged in the wider life of the school. Success criteria KS4 outcomes in 2025/26 will indicate that the gap in Progress 8 scores between FSM 6 and non-FSM pupils in Maths and English will have narrowed to less than 0.5 KS4 outcomes in 2025/26 will show that students with Low PA will achieve a Progress 8 score of at least -0.3 Internal data will show that disadvantaged pupils are making good progress towards their target grades in English and Maths by the end of the academic year. The overall absence gap between disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged pupils being reduced to less than 3%. Evidence of disadvantaged pupils receiving beneficial support and interventions from pastoral support team. Evidence of disadvantaged pupils taking part in extra-curricular activities. 3 Activity in this academic year This details how we intend to spend our pupil premium (and recovery premium funding) this academic year to address the challenges listed above. Teaching (for example, CPD, recruitment and retention) Budgeted cost: £120,200 Activity Overstaffing of English and Maths departments to enable smaller class sizes at KS4. Overstaffing of Maths, Science and Languages to enable smaller class sizes at KS3. Designating a member of staff as the pupil premium co-ordinator. Evidence that supports this approach The EEF toolkit identifies that reducing class sizes can have a positive impact on pupil attainment, if teachers are able to give more individual feedback to learners. Reducing class size | EEF (educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk) The EEF guide to the Pupil Premium emphasises the importance of creating, implementing and monitoring the impact of a long-term strategy. Designating this responsibility to a member of staff ensures that this process is carried out effectively. EEF Pupil Premium Guide 2024 Challenge number(s) addressed 1, 2, 3 1-4 4 Targeted academic support Budgeted cost: £65,000 Activity Homework support room for Year 7 and Year 8 students Academic interventions – GCSE English and Maths Pupil support room Academic interventions – various Year 7 pupil groups Pupil support room LSA interventions with KS3 students in English and Maths Evidence that supports this approach Homework | EEF (educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk) The EEF toolkit stresses the importance of pupils having a quiet space in which to complete homework, and identifies that homework has a beneficial impact particularly on disadvantaged pupils. One to one tuition | EEF (educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk) The EEF identifies individual support as being very effective at improving individual pupils’ outcomes, providing approximately five months’ additional progress on average. Challenge number(s) addressed 3 1, 2 3 Targeted pastoral support Budgeted cost: £65,000 Activity Attendance support – Pupil Support Room Behaviour support – Pupil Support Room SEMH support – Pupil welfare hub Reaching Higher Mentoring Evidence that supports this approach Department for Education (publishing.service.gov.uk) This government report identifies the clear link between improving attendance and improving educational outcomes. Behaviour interventions | EEF (educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk) The EEF toolkit identifies that targeted behaviour interventions have a positive effect on pupils’ progress. Challenge number(s) addressed 4 4, 5 4, 5 4, 5 5 Wider strategies Budgeted cost: £25,000 Activity Evidence that supports this approach Academic materials – textbooks, revision guides etc. Extra-curricular activities, including sport and music activities Duke of Edinburgh Our pupils require academic materials which support them in their learning. All textbooks and revision guides are purchased by the school for all PPG pupils to ensure they have the same access to materials as their peers. www.anewdirection.org.uk/blog/using-pupilpremium-to-enrich-cultural-education Case studies demonstrate enriching cultural capital can help narrow the gap between disadvantaged students and their peers. Challenge number(s) addressed 1-5 4, 5 4, 5 Individual pupil Some pupils require support with equipment 1-5 support – equipment and uniform costs in order to access school. and uniform Total budgeted cost: £ 275,200 6 Part B: Review of outcomes in the previous academic year Pupil premium strategy outcomes This details the impact of our Pupil Premium funding in the 2024-2025 academic year. We have analysed the performance of our school’s disadvantaged pupils during the previous academic year, using national data primarily through FFT Aspire and our own internal data. There is evidence of success in some areas of our strategy. Our vulnerable students have high levels of support available to them, provided by a range of interventions within the Welfare Hub and Pupil Support Room. The provision in both of these areas has been increased by the school in the past academic year, meaning that more students are able to access support for their emotional wellbeing. Our academic interventions have also increased, with more staff employed to support students struggling academically, particularly in English and Maths. We have also increased our staffing in core subjects, so that students can be taught in smaller class sizes for English Maths, Science and Languages. However, it will take time to see the impact of these changes and there remains a gap in the progress of pupils at GCSE compared with their peers. This is still a key area of focus in the strategy statement. The data on attendance shows that whilst the gap between our disadvantaged students and non-disadvantaged students had reduced in the academic year of 2023/24, it has widened again in 2024/25. Improving the attendance of our disadvantaged students , and therefore funding for the Attendance Team remains a priority. Our externally provided mentoring with Reaching Higher has made a positive difference with some of our students who are struggling to engage with school. We have received a strong Impact Report, as well as positive feedback from students involved in the programme. We intend to extend this programme to more pupils in the next academic year. Based on all the information above, the performance of our disadvantaged pupils is meeting expectations in some areas, and we are at present on course to achieve some of the outcomes we set out to achieve by 2025/6. We are not currently on target for reducing the progress gap at GCSE between our disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged pupils and this remains an area of focus for the school. Reducing the attendance gap between our disadvantaged and non-disadvantaged students remains a priority for the school. We are on course to meet our targets of providing extra-curricular activities improving pastoral interventions for our disadvantaged students. Externally provided programmes Programme Reaching Higher mentoring programme Provider Reaching Higher 7 8

documents/pages/religious-studies-2.pdf.text: October 2020 SIXTH FORM Religious Studies A Level Course Overview In Religious Studies there are three ‘strands’ 1. Christianity •Key Issues in the study of the teachings of Jesus, the early church and modern issues in Christianity 2. Ethics •A study of key moral theories such as Utilitarianism and Situation Ethics and how this applies to issues such as homosexuality and nuclear weapons 3. Philosophy •An examination of proofs for the existence of God and the reasons that might count against God’s existence September 2020 What’s great about Religious Studies at Tenison’s Sixth Form? • Helps you develop your evaluation and debating skills • Links well with other subjects • Engages with the existential questions – ‘Why are we here?’ Also questions about faith and morals • Allows you to reflect on and develop your own values • Teaches you to think critically and analytically • Broadens your understanding of other philosophies • Helps with a huge range of careers e.g. law, social work, medicine/nursing, teaching, Christian ministry October 2020 Opportunities and Successes • We have a 100% pass rate in Religious Studies at A Level for the past three years • Last year more than 90% of students achieved an A* to C grade • Former Religious Studies students at Tenison’s have gone on to study degrees at excellent universities such as Edinburgh, Durham and York, • They have read for degrees as diverse as: • Theology and Philosophy • Religious Studies • Law • History September 2020

documents/pages/religious-studies.pdf.text: October 2020 SIXTH FORM: Religious Studies Religious Studies Course Overview Christianity A mixture of philosophy, theology, ethics, history and debates within Christianity. Looking at: - The Trinity - Jesus - The problem of evil - Religious experience Ethics This unit connects to real life scenarios. You will: - Look at actual moral dilemmas - Different ways of thinking about morality - Challenge theories Philosophy You are learning not just what religious and non- religious people believe but whether those beliefs are justified. This includes: - Arguments for God’s existence - The problem of evil - Religious language - Miracles What’s great about Religious Studies at Tenison’s Sixth Form? Within Religious Studies you will learn how to critically engage with a wide range of subject content. You will be comparing arguments, evaluating evidence and, explaining why a philosopher or scholar might be right or wrong. Students develop their debating and discussion skills which are easily translated to other subjects and into University life. It also connects to real-world issues; within Ethics we look at animal rights and euthanasia. Students will also develop their essay-writing skills, complimenting other essay-based subjects.

documents/pages/remote-education-stateme.text: Remote Education Statement At Archbishop Tenison’s CE High School, we are committed to ensuring continuity of education for pupils who are unable to attend onsite for a range of reasons. Remote education will only be implemented as a last resort and should never be viewed as an equal alternative to face-to-face learning. Attendance in school remains essential for pupils’ academic progress, wellbeing and wider life chances, and remote learning will be used only when attending school is not possible but pupils are still able to continue learning. Definition of Remote Education Remote Education refers to learning activities, resources and teacher support provided when lessons cannot take place face to face. This may occur during full or partial school closures, when pupils are absent for a pre-agreed reason, or in cases of pupil exclusion. Short-Term Closures For closures lasting up to five working days, departments will set one task per year group, per subject. Each task will reflect the combined duration of lesson time and homework allocation over one calendar week. All work will be set via Microsoft Teams (MSTeams). Longer-Term Closures For closures lasting more than five working days, a structured timetable of work and live lessons will be shared with families. All resources and live lesson links will be delivered through MSTeams. All remote education will be provided in line with the school’s safeguarding, online safety, and data protection policies. Should there be a long-term closure, more information will be shared. Individual Remote Learning Individual Remote Learning applies when the school remains open, but a pupil is unable to attend in person while still being well enough to work. Parents and carers should liaise with the relevant Head of Year and the Head of Pupil Welfare. Work will then be coordinated by Heads of Department and subject teachers. Families will initially receive our Online Learning Links document, created by Middle Leaders, containing subject-specific websites and online learning platforms. Subject teachers will then provide suitable tasks, shared either directly with parents/carers via email or with pupils via MSTeams. Parents and carers will work collaboratively with the Head of Pupil Welfare to ensure that individual remote learning arrangements remain effective and appropriate. Regular communication will support the monitoring of engagement, identification of any concerns, and exchange of feedback so that provision continues to meet the pupil’s needs. Access to Devices and Connectivity If parents or carers do not have access to an appropriate device or reliable internet connectivity, they should inform the Head of Pupil Welfare as soon as possible. The school will work with families to identify suitable solutions, and paper-based learning materials can be provided where digital access is not available.

The items below marked with * have the school crest and therefore can only be purchased from our School Outfitters: Hewitts of Croydon, Church Street, Croydon www.hewittsofcroydon.com Please note that school blazers and house ties are compulsory items that must be always worn. Jumpers/cardigans are optional items. All other items may be purchased from other retailers. Blazer Shirt Tie Trousers/skirt Jumper/cardigan Socks/tights Shoes Coat Girls Boys Boys and girls: School blazer with school crest * Blue blouse (optional: short sleeves, revereneckline) If not revere, top button must be fastened White shirt (long or short sleeves optional – the top button must be fastened. House tie * – clip on (not required with revere neckline shirt) Girls - House tie – clip on to be worn at all times when wearing a shirt, when wearing blouse no tie is required, white or black socks/beige or black tights. House tie * - clip on – to be worn at all times Mid-grey skirt or mid-grey trousers Mid-grey trousers – must be worn on the waist Tenison’s blue V-neck jumper or cardigan with school crest * (optional item) Tenison’s blue V-neck jumper with the school crest * (optional item) Pupils are also permitted to wear a Tenison’s blue V-neck jumper without the school crest Pupils are also permitted to wear a Tenison’s blue V-neck jumper without the school crest White or black socks or beige or black tights – please note white socks should not be worn over black tights. documents/pages/send-information-report..text: A Parent/ Carer Guide to Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) at Archbishop Tenison’s CE School What is our aim? Archbishop Tenison’s CE School is a Christian community where every individual is valued and where we are concerned to promote the learning and development of all our pupils. We aim to: • Ensure that every pupil at Tenison’s should have access to a broad, balanced and relevant curriculum • Foster a learning environment that enables all children and young adults to reach their full potential • Raise the autonomy and to improve the school life of children with SEND and to recognise and reward their achievements • Educate all pupils and students alongside other pupils and students, recognising the diversity of children’s learning experiences and needs We are committed to supporting children across the four areas of needs. Please see the needs below, however this is not an exhaustive list: Areas of Need Cognition and Learning (CL) Communication and interaction (CI) Social Emotional and Mental Health (SEMH) Physical and Sensory (PH) SEND Conditions Specific Learning Difficulty (SpLD) Moderate Learning Needs (MLD) Dyslexia, Dyscalculia, Dyspraxia DLD and Speech and Language Needs (SLCN) Autism (ASD) ADD, ADHD, Need associated with Trauma and mental wellbeing Disability, Visual Impairment (VI) and Hearing Impairment (HI) Sensory needs. Who should I contact if I want to discuss the needs of my child? The Subject Teacher The Form Tutor The Head of Year or Senior Pastoral Lead • If I have a question about the teaching and learning in a particular subject area • If I want to discuss the personal development of my child • If my child needs support with organisation, self-respect, selfesteem or something similar • If I need to let the school know about a change at home • If I’m not sure who to talk to and would like advice • If I have a concern about my child which is more serious 1 The SEND coordinators: Ms Francesca Ryan Ryanf@archten.croydon.sch.uk Ms Laura Daniel Danil@archten.croydon.sch.uk • If I have a question about the support provided for my child from the SEND department • If I want to discuss a specific intervention program for my child or an alternative curriculum or course How can I find out how well my child is doing? Pastoral Leads, Form Tutors, Subject Teachers and the SENDCOs all monitor student levels to identify students who are not making adequate progress. If you are concerned about the progress of your child or want to find out more about how they are doing outside of the normal reporting process and parents’ evenings, you can contact either their form tutor, the SENDCO or a specific subject teacher. 2 If your child is not making adequate progress, further assessments and discussions with key staff and parents may result in extra support being put into place depending on the individual situation. Pupils and parents are always actively involved in all decisions relating to SEND support and this is documented on pupil Learning Plans and meeting minutes. In some cases, for students who already have Education Health Care Plans, Learning Support Assistant (LSA) support might be allocated. There is always an expectation that all students will develop independent learning skills rather than becoming reliant on adult support. For students on the SEND Support Register, review meetings are held regularly. Parents will be invited annually to a formal review meeting where the level of progress and effectiveness of any support and intervention is evaluated and revised accordingly. If your child continues to make little or no progress, an Education Health Care Plan may be requested. Further details about this process will be explained by the SENDCOs and information will be published in the LA Local Offer. Croydon Local Offer Will my child get special arrangements in tests and exams? For some pupils, additional arrangements and adjustments can be made to enable them to fully access internal and external exams. This might include additional time, rest breaks, reader, prompt, separate rooming, use of a laptop or a scribe. We have a qualified exams access arrangements assessor who can assess and identify which pupils are eligible for additional support in exams. Your child does not qualify for additional arrangements purely because of being on the SEND Support Register. How will the curriculum and learning environment be adapted to meet the needs of my child? Teachers are skilled at adapting the curriculum to meet the diverse range of needs in each class. Daily planning and Quality First Teaching such as differentiating activities, adjusting resources, and providing targeted support (e.g. small group and/or 1:1) ensures that the needs of pupils with SEND are met. Classroom seating plans are carefully considered to optimise access to learning for pupils with SEND. Sensory audits are conducted of learning environments and access for pupils with physical disabilities is ensured. Grouping arrangements are organised flexibly with opportunities for both ability and mixed setting to maximise learning opportunities for all. Additional adults are used flexibly to help groups and individual pupils, with a long-term goal of developing independent learning skills. In addition to planned adaptations in the classroom, the following range of interventions are in place to remove barriers to learning and participating in all aspects of school life: Intervention Cognition & Learning: Literacy and Numeracy Support Cognition & Learning: Quest Reading Program Communication and Interaction: Social Communication Intervention What is It? Small group Literacy and Numeracy Lessons instead of studying French and German. Lessons are with one of the SEND team. 2 form times each week to develop students’ reading and spelling skills – with an LSA 1 form time a week with an LSA using the ‘Talkabout for Teenagers’ intervention scheme 3 Communication and Interaction: Emotional Literacy Support Assistant (ELSA) Social, Emotional and Mental Health: Haven Lunchtime Club Social, Emotional and Mental health: SEND homework club Social, Emotional and Mental Health: Transition Nurture Group Social, Emotional and Mental Health: Mental Health Support Team (MHST) Social, Emotional and Mental Health: Welfare Hub Sensory and/or Physical: Sensory Circuits 1 lesson a week for a set number of weeks with our ELSA on either a 1:1 or small group basis Supervised games club to eat and chat with friends A quiet space to complete homework with support from an LSA. Access to computers and a printer. 6 Small Group sessions in September – October to aid transition for our most vulnerable pupils – with an LSA 1 session a week for 6 weeks to support a range of SEMH issues – with an appropriately trained member of staff Access to the Welfare Hub throughout the school day – with the Assistant Head of Pupil Welfare and Lay Chaplain 2 sessions a week in the Sports Hall with equipment – with two LSAs How skilled are staff at meeting the needs of my child? An on-going programme of training is in place to ensure that all teachers and support staff have appropriate skills and knowledge to support provision for children with SEND. Recent training for new teachers has covered adaptive teaching and trauma-informed practice as well as specific training for teachers about our pupils with Visual Impairments. Our SENDCOs actively engage in a range of opportunities to share best practice and keep abreast of current local and national initiatives and policies to support pupils with SEND. Careful planning and risk-assessments take place for physical activities and trips to ensure that all important that all pupils can access all opportunities on offer. When required, the governing body may involve health and social services bodies, local authority support services and voluntary organisations to help meet the needs of pupils SEND and support their families. The school also seeks advice and guidance from local special schools to review, evaluate and develop provision for pupils who have the most complex needs. What support from outside does the school use to help support my child? The school works with a number of external agencies to seek advice and support to ensure that the needs of all children are fully understood and met. These include: Agency Educational Psychology Service Our attached Educational Psychologist is Dr Jo Blanchard. Speech and Language Therapy Description of support Observations of students, advice on teaching and support strategies. Meetings with students and parents. Assessment on needs. Referral to outside agencies where appropriate. Advice on intervention, teaching and support strategies for pupils with EHCPs. CAMHS (Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service) Advice on intervention, teaching and support strategies. Additional support and assessment on need where appropriate. 4 Virtual School for Children who are Looked After virtualschool@croydon.gov.uk Hearing Impairment Service Visual Impairment Service Croydon Early Help Team Mental Health Schools Team This service oversees and monitors provision for children who are in the care of the Local Authority Advice on intervention, teaching and support strategies. Additional support and assessment where necessary. Advice on intervention, teaching and support strategies. Additional support and assessment where necessary. Advice on intervention and signposting to other agencies for support Advice and support on strategic school intervention on mental health and wellbeing. How will the school help my child in the transition from Primary to Secondary or when moving to or from another school? Children and young people with SEND can become particularly anxious about ‘moving on’ so we seek to support successful transition. When moving to another school: We will contact the school SENDCO and share information about special arrangements and support that has been made to help your child achieve their learning goals. We will ensure that all records are passed on as soon as possible including exam access arrangements documents. In Year 6 /7 Transition A member of the transition team attends the Primary to Secondary Transition day meeting to discuss the specific needs of your child and the nature and level of support which has had the most impact. In some cases additional multi-agency meetings may be arranged to create a more detailed ‘transition’ plan which may include more visits to or from Archbishop Tenison’s School. Every student with an Education Health Plan is offered a one-to-one tour of the school before the summer and the opportunity to meet key staff. Further information about support and services for families can be found at https://localoffer.croydon.gov.uk/kb5/croydon/directory/home.page Contact details of support services for parents of pupils with SEND: Croydon SENDIASS team - 020 8663 5630, croydon@kids.org.uk for impartial advice Croydon SEN Team (senenquiries@croydon.gov.uk) for EHCP and school support Complaints Any complaints concerning SEND provision should be dealt with in line with the school Complaints Procedure. Our full SEND policy is available from the school on request. 5 Updated: March 2026 6

documents/pages/siams.pdf.text: Statutory Inspection of Anglican and Methodist Schools (SIAMS) Report Archbishop Tenison’s Church of England High School Vision Our vision is rooted in 1 Corinthians 13:13, ‘these three remain: faith, hope and love’. This links to our vision for education where pupils grow up ‘in every way…into Christ’, where every pupil makes a vital contribution to the whole (Ephesians 4:14-16). These are embodied in our motto ‘Tenaciter – Academic excellence for each person as part of a Christian community’. Archbishop Tenison’s Church of England High School is living up to its foundation as a Church school and is enabling pupils and adults to flourish. It has the following notable strengths. Notable Strengths • The biblically rooted vision is the bedrock upon which this Church school has grown. Leaders evaluate its Christian distinctiveness effectively and make bold strategic decisions that enable pupils to flourish academically and personally. • Prayer and worship are the heartbeat of the school and are a hallmark of its distinctiveness. Rich opportunities for varied and spontaneous times of prayer and worship abound. Consequently, pupils and adults grow spiritually as they explore Bible stories and embrace the value of stillness and reflection for themselves. • A sense of hope and belonging is carefully developed which is driven by expansive and effective chaplaincy and pastoral provision. Its impact is profound. Pupils are treasured and their unique worth embraced by adults who model the love of God through their caring and nurturing actions. • Academic support given by adults breaks down barriers to learning for pupils, including those who have special educational needs and/or disabilities (SEND) and those who are vulnerable. Consequently, pupils thrive as they seek to pursue their unique gifts and talents. • Leaders’ extensive support for staff ensures that they feel highly valued and well cared for. As a result, they flourish professionally and personally. Development Points • Embed the shared understanding of spirituality. This is so that pupils can experience rich opportunities for spiritual development within the curriculum as well as through collective worship. • Refine the Year 9 religious education (RE) curriculum. This is so that pupils have opportunities to apply their knowledge of a range of religions and worldviews beyond Christianity. Inspection Findings Vision and Leadership The vision, rooted in biblical teaching, is foundational to the success of this flourishing secondary school. Leaders carefully harness the school’s 300-year-old history and purpose to shape its ongoing strategic direction. They are single-minded in ensuring that the school’s Christian foundation remains relevant to its context today. The focus upon a Christian understanding of ‘faith, hope and love’ underpins its distinctiveness as a Church school. These virtues continue to shape the school’s community and the lives of the pupils it serves, including those who have SEND and/or are vulnerable. Leaders evaluate the impact of the vision extremely effectively and make bold strategic decisions as a result. For example, to expand the school to offer more opportunities for those families who wish to attend a secondary school with a specifically Christian ethos. Alongside a strong focus on building academic success, leaders place significant emphasis on pupils equally growing in their character, using Jesus as the example. Consequently, pupils have hope for their future and actively care for those around them. Vision and Curriculum The vision is lived out as pupils strive for excellence in their learning and through the wider opportunities that the school offers. To support pupils to learn, leaders have created well used quiet study spaces within the Sixth Form area and a new library resource. Additionally, adults inspire curiosity through engaging methods of teaching and highly valued resources. They skilfully modify approaches for pupils, including those who have SEND and those who are disadvantaged. Teachers support pupils well and careful attention is given to those who find learning more challenging. Through a wide range of sensitively designed programmes, staff expertly design activities that help pupils to develop as tenacious learners. For example, through the provision of homework clubs, smaller learning spaces and targeted groups to support literacy and numeracy. Consequently, learning potential is carefully cultivated. The school offers a broad extra-curricular programme including sports, performing and expressive arts as well as visits. These are instrumental in enabling pupils to pursue their Godgiven talents. Furthermore, the school has recently refined its shared understanding of spiritual development. Some curriculum areas, such as English, are beginning to embed opportunities for spiritual discovery within their lessons. However, this is at an early stage of implementation within other subject areas. As a result, this limits the way that the curriculum extends pupils’ spiritual development. Worship and Spirituality Exuberant and vibrant daily times of togetherness are an integral part of collective worship at Archbishop Tenison’s. These times are greatly valued by pupils and staff who enthusiastically lead worship. Strong partnerships with a variety of local churches enable pupils to encounter broad and diverse styles of worship. The school’s worship band leads joyful and uplifting times of singing. As a result, pupils and adults value this time which enriches their spiritual development. Worship is carefully planned and coordinated by the Chaplaincy team. They creatively develop highly effective resources that are relevant to the lives of adults and pupils. Prayer and times of reflection are the heartbeat of the school. Outside of the daily planned times of worship, pupils have opportunities to pray at the start of each lesson. Furthermore, pupils in the Sixth Form offer opportunities to gather each week for prayer, and well as before exams. Many pupils consider this important to their own personal strength and wellness. Consequently, both pupils and adults spiritually flourish through dedicated time to explore Jesus’ teachings and through open opportunities to respond. Pupils point to these times of worship as pivotal to their own character development. They value them as a central feature of the school’s daily life. Religious Education RE is valued and is prioritised by leaders. With effective support from the diocese, the RE curriculum has been overhauled to enhance its relevance to pupils. Therefore, they now explore in greater depth the differing ways in which people think about, and practise, their beliefs. The curriculum is planned effectively to develop pupils’ critical writing skills as they progress through the school. Consequently, they are enthusiastic about their The National Society Church of England and Church in Wales) for the Promotion of Education is a registered charity (313070) in England and Wales learning and demonstrate strong subject-specific vocabulary. They point to RE as fundamental in developing their understanding towards those of different faiths and worldviews. As a result, pupils feel well prepared for life in a multi-cultural society. Almost all pupils study for the full GCSE qualification, following the foundation that is built in Key Stage 3. In the Sixth Form, they value the opportunity to study A level philosophy and ethics. Leaders have thought successfully about the core RE provision for those not studying the A level. Building on relevant religious and ethical themes, Sixth Form pupils explore healthy debate around difficult topics such as assisted dying. The curriculum enables pupils to develop a deepening understanding of different faiths, particularly Christianity. However, in Year 9, pupils’ knowledge of a range of religions and worldviews is less secure. This is because, beyond the study of Christianity, there are fewer opportunities for pupils to explore and apply their prior learning from Years 7 and 8. The quality of teaching of RE is strong. Teachers deliver high-quality learning focused on answering big questions, such as ‘what is morality?’ Pupils benefit from engaging activities, which support them to remember what they have learnt. Consequently, they make strong progress in their learning. At GCSE and A level, teachers skilfully use assessment and feedback to ensure that misconceptions are picked up quickly and addressed. Therefore, pupils achieve well in external examinations. Vision, Justice and Responsibility The Christian vision drives a culture of service towards others where pupils can make a ‘vital contribution to the whole’. Guided by the vision, leaders meaningfully plan opportunities to develop pupils’ understanding of personal and community responsibility. Sixth Form ambassadors demonstrate strong leadership skills as they inspire pupils in lower year groups to make positive changes. For example, to help younger pupils to settle, they actively support those in Year 7 to become proactive anti-bullying ambassadors. Equally, to tackle loneliness, older pupils mentor younger peers and are a source of support at social times. Within the taught curriculum, well-chosen topics enable pupils to grow as caring community members. For instance, within A level business studies lessons they explore unethical exploitation within industries. More widely, pupils are empowered to take proactive action against the causes of injustice. For example, they tackle food poverty by supporting and distributing food at the local food bank. Additionally, pupil leaders advocate for causes that are important to them. Learning about injustice in the treatment of women motivated them to design a bake sale to raise awareness about this. The vision and associated values help pupils to understand the link between faith and action. Consequently, they value the importance of showing responsibility towards each other and serving their local communities. Vision and School Culture Inspired by the message of hope in the Bible, leaders carefully craft a culture centred upon their understanding of God’s love for all. It is a core feature of the transition programme taught in Year 7. This helps pupils to understand what belonging and community mean at Archbishop Tenison’s. Weekly pastoral studies lessons, alongside relevant collective worship themes, devote time to exploring and applying teachings from the Bible. This enables pupils to consider how they might play their own unique part in building this inclusive and caring community. Chaplaincy and pastoral support for pupils and families is extensive. They are extremely proactive in developing wide-ranging nurture groups to support individuals and groups of pupils. For example, the welfare hub is a highly effective source of comfort. Driven by the Christian vision, the school provides greatly valued support to those facing challenging circumstances. Adults prize pupils’ unique worth and cherish those within their care, including the most vulnerable. Equally, adults appreciate the care they are shown by leaders personally and in their roles. They additionally welcome the spiritual support given through daily prayers and encouragement. Furthermore, through extensive training opportunities, adults grow in confidence as they develop professionally. Consequently, staff are highly valued and well cared for. documents/pages/sixthformsubjectoverview.text: October 2020 SIXTH FORM MFL A Level Course Overview • We teach French and German and offer non-taught courses for some languages for native speakers (as long as an Alevel exists), we follow the AQA specification • In year 12 we talk about trends in the culture of the TL such as the changing nature of family, film and music, heritage technology and tourism. • In year 13 we deal with more academic topics, such as immigration and integration, politics and history. • We study a film and a book in the target language and learn what this reveals about the country and its culture. • There is also an independent research project, where you choose a topic of interest to you and research it. This is really great practice for university and independent study skills. September 2020 What’s great about MFL at Tenison’s Sixth Form? • specialist staff and native speakers, • small intimate classes of engaged learners • links to the target language country • chances for independent study generated by your own interests • great results September 2020 Opportunities and Successes • Results • ALPS 2019 French 4 (very good); no German ALPS 2020 French 3 (excellent); German 2 (outstanding) • Career Opportunities • tourism, import export, any career that requires communication with good/services abroad, foreign market banking, anything abroad where the language is spoken, teaching, etc. • Speaking a second language boosts your employability in any sector!! • the languages most often sought by employers are: French, German, Spanish, Chinese (Mandarin), Arabic. Source: 2018 report from the CBI, a lobbying organisation that represents British businesses

documents/pages/ten-things-about-tenison.text: things you may not know about Archbishop Tenison’s Church of England High School 1 A Strong TRADITION 310 years of combining Christian character and academic purpose. Thought to be the longest running mixed school under the same foundation. “The distinctiveness and effectiveness of Archbishop Tenison’s as a Church of England School are outstanding.” Siams Report 2 An Excellent TRACK RECORD 2023 ATTAINMENT 8 Tenison’s England Average 47.1 46.3 E BACC AVERAGE 4.23 4.05 3 A Successful TRANSITION PROGRAMME into the school and Sixth Form “The great sense of community and welcoming atmosphere ensured the transition from my previous school was seamless.” Erica, Year 12 4 Dynamic TEACHING in a well-established, focused learning community ‘High-quality teaching, effective leadership and consistently high expectations have ensured that all groups of students achieve exceptionally well.’ Ofsted 5 Thoughtful TEAMWORK AND COMMUNICATION “Archbishop Tenison’s has an excellent Sixth Form which enriches students – both academically and socially. The Sixth Form Leadership roles available allow students to make a real difference to the wider community of the school.” Simon, Year 13 9 ENJOYMENT of Study “This school, with its unwavering commitment to excellence, provides the perfect foundation for students to strive, both academically and personally.” Princess, Year 13 10 CONFIDENCE to Succeed in different walks of life “Tenison’s has shaped me as a person. Not only does the school aim for success academically, but the school has a fantastic support system and pupils are encouraged to follow their ambitions. I am very proud to be a Sixth Form student here.” Neriah, Year 13 8 High INVOLVEMENT in our many, varied extra-curricular activities Year groups have teams in football, basketball, netball, rugby league (boys and girls), cricket and rounders. Clubs include Year 7 choir and gospel choir, cookery, debating, chess, Haven, drama, art, Duke of Edinburgh and Green Team/gardening. 6 A Knowledgeable, Literate CURRICULUM A good foundation for life and study 16 subject choices are available at GCSE. Over 20 subject choices are offered at A-Level. 7 Shared Excitement, INTEREST AND OPPORTUNITIES in all the different subjects we teach, co-curricular activities include trips to Berlin, Ypres, The British Film Institute and skiing. Our Aim Archbishop Tenison’s Church of England High School exists to provide a Church of England education, primarily for children of Anglican and other Christian families living within the Archdeaconry of Croydon and Deanery of Sutton. Our Ethos Archbishop Tenison’s has a distinctive Christian ethos, which gives the school its purpose and provides an inclusive environment, where children can learn and flourish in a setting shaped by Christian values. We welcome applications from all members of the community and we ask all parents to respect the Christian ethos of the school. We value five things in particular; courtesy, calmness, concentration, confidence and consideration. Our Purpose Together with Church schools across the world we seek to educate the whole person. Our curriculum combines the academic, the human and the practical; our teaching develops the knowledge, understanding and skills of each pupil across all the different subjects; our pupils learn best in a community where they know and are known - and where they find the space to think independently, the grace to understand new and difficult things and the inner strength to succeed. This is what it takes for academic study to be rewarding and, above all, enjoyable. There is much for us to learn as human beings – about ourselves, created in God’s image; about the world in which we live and our purpose in being here; about our relationships with other people and how we handle the differences between us. A good school provides a good start in all of this. Archbishop Tenison’s Alumni include: EMMA BRETON Musical Theatre Actress JOSHUA BUATSI British Professional Boxer MARK BUTCHER Retired England Cricketer GARY CARR Actor CLARE CHAMBERS Novelist THE RIGHT REVD STEPHEN CONWAY Bishop of Ely OLIVER DOVEY Junior Sous-Chef, Claridges JORDAN EDWARDS-WILKS (JORDS) British Singer and Rapper GILLIAN HIBBS Illustrator and Author TWINELLE HOPESON Sprinter ANDREW KING Assistant Producer at BBC Radio 3 KAYLA MEIKLE Actress THE REVD DR JEREMY MORRIS British Historian THOMAS NIELSON Co-Principal Trumpet of the London Philharmonic Orchestra ADAM PEARSON Actor, Presenter and Campaigner JOE PETTITT Band Leader of The Len Phillips Big Band RYAN REID Actor BRYONY SMITH Surrey and England Cricketer Selborne Road, Croydon, CR0 5JQ • Tel. 020 8688 4014 • www.archten.croydon.sch.uk /archtencroydon @archten archbishoptenisons Find out more

documents/pages/theatre-studies.pdf.text: October 2020 DRAMA DEPARTMENT THEATRE STUDIES A LEVEL • In Theatre Studies, we develop your performance and analytical skills. You learn how to work in a group and on your own initiative. • We study a range of plays and practitioners, both ancient and modern practically, rather than just by reading the text! • Our students always enjoy our acting classes where we explore different styles, including physical theatre, stage combat and the preparation of monologues – very useful for auditions! • Our performance exams take place with a small audience in the Drama Studio. October 2020 WHAT’S GREAT ABOUT THEATRE STUDIES AT TENISON’S? • There are two experienced Drama teachers at Tenison’s who share all classes – and we love our subject! We combine practical lessons where we act, and written lessons where we complete coursework and prepare for the written exam. • We use lighting, sound, staging, makeup, costume etc to enhance performance in our Studio. We work closely as a group to develop everyone’s confidence and ability. • Our students really enjoy the safe space we have in Drama and the open discussions we have around text and theme. They work as a close group and form great friendships. October 2020 OPPORTUNITIES AND SUCCESSES • We put on an annual Whole School Show – usually a musical. • We run trips to see theatre performances, recently we have seen ‘Wicked’, ‘A Midsummer Night’s Dream’ and ‘The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-time.’ • In addition to the curriculum, we teach you really useful public speaking and confidence building as well as audition preparation. You have the opportunity to explore technical aspect of theatre, such as lighting, sound and costume. • We have a number of alumni who are currently acting in TV, film and theatre. • Theatre Studies prepares you for a career in the arts but also gives you personal skills valued by all employers. October 2020

documents/pages/transition-journey.pdf.text: YOUR TRANSITION JOURNEY SEPTEMBER TO OCTOBER Visit Archbishop Tenison’s for an Open Event You will have the opportunity to come and explore our school community. You will hear from the Headteacher and other key members of staff, meet subject teachers and have the opportunity to take part in different activities. The transition team will be available to answer any questions about moving to secondary school. MAY TO JUNE Meeting you at your Primary School Where there are several pupils joining from the same school, we will arrange to come and visit you at your primary school. This will give you the opportunity to ask questions and for staff to get to know you. Your teachers will provide information to help plan individual support. JUNE Ice Breaker Session For those of you joining alone or with only one or two pupils from your school, you will be invited to an ice breaker session. This will give you the opportunity to get to know some other pupils before the Transition Day in July. SEPTEMBER Year 7 Induction Before the start of term, there will be an Induction Day for Year 7 pupils. You will meet your tutor group, have your school photograph taken, get familiar with the school environment and key members of staff. SEPTEMBER Beginning of Term Service Your parents/carers will be invited to join us for the Beginning of Term Service at St. Matthew’s Church. OCTOBER Apply for a place at Archbishop Tenison’s During October parents/ carers will apply for a place at Archbishop Tenison’s. Please see the admissions page on our website for more information. Deadline for applications is 31 October each year. MARCH National Offers Day/Website Transition Page goes live If applicable, parents/carers will receive a letter offering you a place at Archbishop Tenison’s. They will also receive an email regarding completion of the online admission forms. A transition page on our website will provide all information, including a welcome video. Deadline for completion of the online admission forms is April. JUNE SEN/Support Transition Day Some pupils will be invited for additional transition support based on information from primary schools. JULY Transition Day You will have the opportunity to come into Archbishop Tenison’s to meet key staff, experience lessons and school life, and meet other pupils joining Tenison’s in September. SEPTEMBER Team Building Day at Frylands Wood Scout Outdoor Centre At the beginning of term, we will head off site to Frylands Wood Scout Outdoor Centre for a team building day, giving you the opportunity to develop friendships and get to know your form group better.

documents/pages/using-the-fob-for-school.text: FRESH FOOD New Fobs We are delighted to confirm the appointment of Independent Catering as your new catering company. Not only will your school food be improved with fresh food, but the technology for the cashless system will be updated to a proximity contactless fob. This can be placed on your key ring. This move will stop you having to touch a pad, as it recognises the fob rather than your finger. The contactless proximity fobs will be issued on the first day of term and linked to cashless accounts online. Fobs are linked to photographs so can only be used by the student to whom they are issued. This move will speed up queues and stop contact of fingers at the tills. The initial fob is free, with replacement fobs charged at £3, so please ensure they are placed on a keyring. All payments should be made online. We no longer have a machine that takes cash to avoid any contact. Thankyou

documents/pages/view-our-prospectus-here.text: Archbishop Tenison’s We are delighted to have the opportunity to tell you about Archbishop Tenison’s. We are a school with a distinctive character and purpose. Our school motto is ‘Academic excellence for each person in a Christian community’ and we aim to instil these values in everything that goes on at Tenison’s. We want our pupils to experience a genuine, strong, Christian learning community. We want our teaching to be rigorous, imaginative and exciting, alive and alert to what interests them. We want to help them develop into people of good character, who can think hard, communicate well and understand for themselves different areas of human experience. We want to see them progress individually, but also grow spiritually and contribute socially – to the school now and in society later. “The school’s ethos makes a strong contribution to students’ spiritual, moral, social and cultural development”. Ofsted A School with a History Our school was founded by Thomas Tenison, Archbishop of Canterbury, in 1714. He wanted to give “ten poor boys and ten poor girls” a good basic education to help them earn an honest living and grow in the Christian faith. Over 300 years later we are on our third site in Croydon and still providing schooling of a high standard in a Christian context. We do this as an 11-18 voluntary aided, Anglican, mixed comprehensive school, within both the Diocese of Southwark and the Borough of Croydon, with Foundation Governors appointed by the Church of England. A School with a Purpose With over 300 years’ experience we are able to approach the challenges of educating young people in the 21st century with clarity of vision and confidence of purpose. We know that the whole person matters, that the best curriculum combines the academic, the human and the practical and that the best teaching develops the knowledge, understanding and skills of each pupil across all the different subjects. We also know that the best learning takes place in a school community where pupils know and are known and where they find the space to learn independently, the grace to understand new and difficult things and the inner strength to succeed. This is what it takes for their academic study to be rewarding and, above all, enjoyable. We recognise that there is so much for us to learn as human beings – about ourselves as created in God’s image; about the world in which we live and our purpose in being here; and about our relationships with other people and how we handle the differences between us. Teaching and Learning The curriculum at Archbishop Tenison’s retains a particular focus on the core subjects of English, Maths, Science and Modern Languages, with a high profile for History, Geography and Religious Studies, as well as a lively tradition of Art, Computing, Drama, Music, Physical Education and different forms of Technology. In the Sixth Form we add social science courses in Business Studies, Economics, Politics, Psychology and Sociology, as well as Spanish and the Extended Project. Personal and Social Development is taught in every year. Good teaching is at the heart of all that we do. Our school motto of “Academic excellence for each person in a Christian community” means that every lesson matters. High standards of discipline and pace ensure each pupil fulfils his or her potential in a class setting. Imaginative resources, wellstructured discourse and good teamwork between staff and pupils make for challenging and engaging tasks. Success is celebrated, effort rewarded and achievement recognised. Good provision is made for Gifted and Talented pupils and for those with Special Educational Needs. “High quality teaching, effective leadership and consistently high expectations have ensured that all groups of students achieve exceptionally well”. Ofsted Extra-Curricular Activities There is a remarkable number of different curricular and extra-curricular activities at Tenison’s. We have a strong tradition of music and of drama. The orchestra, gospel choir, chamber choir, other groups and choirs are well supported; many pupils have instrumental tuition. Our concerts and school productions are of a very high standard. We have a great tradition of competitive sport athletics, cricket, cross-country, football, netball, rounders, rugby and tennis. We do well at debating and public speaking and in the UK and European Maths Challenges. We run Geography and Biology Field Visits, a Duke of Edinburgh programme, two vibrant exchanges with Rouen and Berlin and numerous trips – ranging from skiing to water sports, from a Christian residential weekend to a day visit to Bodiam Castle. Our Sixth Form Soirée and other events for charity are well supported. Support and Guidance We work hard at ensuring a good transition for pupils from Year 6 to Year 7. Our pastoral care is strong, with each pupil belonging to a Tutor Group and one of four Houses named after Archbishops of Canterbury. Good relationships make other things possible, including a high standard of self-discipline amongst pupils and the mutual respect and understanding which are the prerequisite for academic success. There are good vertical links across year groups and older pupils act as strong and positive role models with the School Council, House Captains and Sixth Form Student Leaders and mentors all playing a key role in the life of the school as a whole community. There is a friendly competition between Houses, formal celebration of achievements at annual Year Presentation Evenings and a determination on everyone’s part to be good “Tenisonians”. “The vibrant Christian community in action, where pupils and staff are cared for as individuals”. SIAMS Communication Good communication with parents is a high priority for us, recognising the important role which parents and carers have in supporting their child’s education. Year group information evenings are held at the start of each year. Formal progress checks are issued each half term and a full report once a year. As well as traditional parents’ evenings, we hold subject and revision evenings so that parents can understand better how to provide support at home. Homework is integral to good learning and has to be completed promptly and done well. Parents are invited to join the Archbishop Tenison’s Parents’ Association (ATPA), which gives strong, vibrant support to school events and fund-raising. “Communication between the school and parents is very effective and well managed”. Year 11 Parent Special Educational Needs Pupils are assessed on transition and provision for those with special needs is co-ordinated and monitored by the school’s SEN and Learning Support department. Pupils also learn about other major world religions. All pupils take the GCSE for which they study Mark’s Gospel and a range of contemporary moral issues. In the Sixth Form there are themed awaydays as well as the opportunity to study A-Level Theology, Philosophy and Ethics. “Diverse opportunities and expressions of worship that have a significant impact on the school community and are highly valued by pupils, staff, parents and governors”. SIAMS Assemblies and Church Services Each year begins and each term ends with a service at St. Matthew’s Church, where we also hold interdenominational Communion Services once a year for each year group. Parents are warmly invited to our Carol Service and Founder’s Day Services. Our Chaplain is the Vicar of St. Matthew’s. Personal and Social Education There is a varied programme of lessons and activities. This includes provision for Sex and Health Education, giving pupils an insight into Christian principles of moral responsibility for oneself and one’s neighbour. Parents have the right to withdraw their child from these lessons. For Careers Education and Guidance there are taught lessons, opportunities for individual interviews, work experience and access to the careers library. Religious Education The teaching is in accordance with that of the Church of England and is based on the Southwark Diocesan scheme and the Croydon agreed syllabus. Assemblies in school are held daily and are predominantly Christian, in keeping with the school’s foundation. Parents have the right to withdraw their child from Religious Studies and collective worship. The Sixth Form In the Sixth Form we offer a wide range of A Levels as well as one BTEC. A separate prospectus is available on request.
